questions.stem: Before colonisation, many Aboriginal peoples used fire as a tool for caring for Country. Which description of this practice is most accurate?
options: Rare, intense fires lit only during ceremonies to clear land permanently
Fires lit mainly to drive neighbouring groups away from shared hunting grounds
Large summer wildfires set each year to destroy forest and leave bare ground
Frequent, cool, patchy burns that kept country open and renewed food plants
questions.explanation: Cultural burning was planned and regular: cool, patchy fires in the right season created a mosaic of burnt and unburnt country, encouraged fresh growth and drew game. It was not aimed at destroying forest or lit only in rare ceremonies.

questions.stem: The term 'fire-stick farming', used to describe Aboriginal burning practices, was coined in 1969 by the archaeologist:
options: Tim Flannery
Rhys Jones
Bill Gammage
Bruce Pascoe
questions.explanation: Rhys Jones introduced the phrase in a 1969 article, arguing that Aboriginal burning had reshaped Australian vegetation. Bill Gammage developed a related argument much later, in The Biggest Estate on Earth (2011).

questions.stem: At Budj Bim in western Victoria, the Gunditjmara people built channels, weirs and ponds in the lava flows of a volcano. These works were designed mainly to:
options: trap, hold and harvest kooyang (short-finned eels)
irrigate fields of murnong through the dry summer
store drinking water for large gatherings in drought
drain swamps to make open kangaroo-hunting ground
questions.explanation: The Gunditjmara engineered the lava flows to direct water and kooyang into traps and holding ponds, so eels could be caught and stored across the seasons. Murnong grew on open plains and was not irrigated by these works.

questions.stem: In 2019 the Budj Bim Cultural Landscape was inscribed on the World Heritage List. Why is this significant for historians of Aboriginal land management?
options: It recognised an engineered Aboriginal aquaculture system thousands of years old
It showed that the Gunditjmara had abandoned fishing in favour of farming crops
It was the first Australian site to be listed for its natural rather than cultural values
It confirmed that colonists had preserved the eel traps on their pastoral runs
questions.explanation: Budj Bim was listed for its Aboriginal cultural values: a system of channels, weirs and ponds built and maintained over thousands of years. Australia's first World Heritage listings, in 1981, were made decades earlier, so it was not the first natural listing; and pastoral occupation damaged rather than preserved the system.

questions.stem: Wil-im-ee Moor-ring (Mount William), near Lancefield in Victoria, was a Wurundjeri quarry that supplied:
options: ochre used only in local Wurundjeri ceremonies at the site
flint for spear points traded north to the Torres Strait
sandstone for grindstones used along the Murray River
greenstone for axe heads traded across south-eastern Australia
questions.explanation: Greenstone from Mount William was shaped into axe heads that travelled through exchange networks far across south-eastern Australia. The quarry shows organised resource use and long-distance trade, not a purely local supply.

questions.stem: Access to the Mount William quarry was controlled by Wurundjeri senior men, and visiting groups received stone under agreed protocols. A historian would most likely use this evidence to argue that:
options: Aboriginal people had no concept of rights over particular places or materials
the quarry was opened in response to demand for axes from European settlers
stone tools were made mainly for trade with Macassan visitors from the north
Aboriginal societies had systems of ownership and responsibility for resources
questions.explanation: Controlled access and rules of exchange show that the quarry was owned and managed under Aboriginal law. This evidence directly undercuts the colonial assumption that the land belonged to no one. The quarry was worked long before Europeans arrived.

questions.stem: The stone fish traps on the Barwon River at Brewarrina, known as Baiame's Ngunnhu, are significant because:
options: they were built by colonists using Aboriginal labour during the 1840s
they were used only to hold water for travelling stock in times of drought
they were deliberately dismantled by the Ngemba to stop colonists fishing
they were shared by several groups under rules for using and maintaining them
questions.explanation: In Ngemba tradition the ancestral being Baiame gave the traps to the people, and families held responsibility for particular pools, with neighbouring groups invited to use them. The traps are an Aboriginal structure of great age, not a colonial one, and colonists later damaged parts of them.

questions.stem: Which development drove the most rapid European occupation of Aboriginal land in south-eastern Australia in the 1830s and 1840s?
options: The Selection Acts, which opened Crown land to small farming families
Irrigation settlements founded along the banks of the Murray River
The spread of squatters' sheep and cattle runs beyond official limits
The gold rushes, which drew miners into the interior in large numbers
questions.explanation: Squatters drove flocks and herds far beyond the official Limits of Location, taking up vast runs and the water on them. The gold rushes began in 1851, the Selection Acts in the 1860s and Murray irrigation settlements in the 1880s, so none fits the 1830s and 1840s.

questions.stem: In 1836 Major Thomas Mitchell named the fertile country of western Victoria 'Australia Felix'. What effect did his published account have?
options: It discouraged settlement by describing the region as a dry desert
It encouraged squatters to overland stock into the Western District
It persuaded the government to reserve the region for Aboriginal people
It led directly to the founding of the Port Phillip settlement in 1835
questions.explanation: Mitchell's glowing description of well-watered grassland drew squatters and their flocks south from New South Wales soon afterwards. His expedition came after the 1835 settlement at Port Phillip, so it could not have caused it.

questions.stem: Explorers and settlers often described open, grassy country with scattered trees as looking like 'a gentleman's park'. In The Biggest Estate on Earth, Bill Gammage argued that such landscapes were:
options: the result of megafauna grazing that ended tens of thousands of years earlier
created by early pastoralists who cleared the trees for their sheep
made and maintained by Aboriginal people, chiefly through planned burning
natural grasslands that no people had altered before 1788
questions.explanation: Gammage argued that in 1788 Aboriginal people managed the continent as one estate, using fire to keep grass and trees in deliberate patterns that made resources plentiful and predictable. On his reading, what settlers saw as natural parkland was a made landscape that already existed when they arrived.

questions.stem: Within a few years of sheep arriving in the Port Phillip District, murnong (yam daisy), a staple Aboriginal food, had become scarce. The main cause was:
options: sheep eating the plants and their hooves compacting the soil
Aboriginal people giving up murnong in favour of rationed flour
a long drought that killed the plants across the whole district
colonists digging up murnong to feed convict work gangs
questions.explanation: Sheep grazed the murnong fields and their hard hooves packed down soils that had been kept soft by digging. Losing this staple pushed Aboriginal people towards dependence on rations, which followed the loss of food rather than causing it.

questions.stem: Which was an environmental consequence of alluvial gold mining in central Victoria in the 1850s?
options: Creeks choked with sludge and hillsides stripped of trees
Widespread salinity from irrigating wheat farms near the diggings
Coastal wetlands drained to build new ports for gold ships
The extinction of the koala across the colony of Victoria
questions.explanation: Washing and sluicing for gold sent sediment into creeks, while trees were cut for timber and fuel, leaving bare, eroding ground. Irrigation-driven salinity came later and elsewhere, and the koala did not become extinct in Victoria.

questions.stem: A historian notes that by the 1860s much of the forest around Ballarat and Bendigo had been cut. Which explanation best accounts for this?
options: The government ordered clearing to prevent a repeat of Black Thursday
Miners burned the bush to expose quartz reefs at the surface
Mines needed props, fuel for steam engines and timber for buildings
Squatters cleared the forest to stop miners crossing their runs
questions.explanation: As mining moved underground, it needed huge quantities of timber for shaft supports and firewood for boilers, while growing towns needed building timber. The cutting was driven by mining demand, not by fire-prevention policy or squatters.

questions.stem: Black Thursday, 6 February 1851, refers to:
options: a flood on the Yarra River that swept away early Melbourne
bushfires that burned a large part of what became Victoria
the day gold was first found in payable amounts at Ballarat
a dust storm that buried crops across South Australia
questions.explanation: On 6 February 1851, fires driven by hot northerly winds swept across much of the Port Phillip District, which became the colony of Victoria later that year. Gold was found in payable amounts in Victoria some months afterwards.

questions.stem: Which combination of conditions contributed to the Black Thursday fires of 1851?
options: Extreme heat and strong northerly winds after a long dry spell
Cool southerly winds fanning fires lit at the new goldfields
A wet summer followed by lightning storms in the cold of winter
Winter burning by squatters that spread through the next spring
questions.explanation: The fires came on a day of extreme heat and strong, hot northerly winds after a long dry period. The Victorian gold rush had not begun in February 1851, and the fires were a summer event.

questions.stem: William Strutt, who lived in Melbourne in 1851, completed a large painting of Black Thursday in 1864. As a source on the fires, the painting is most useful as evidence of:
options: how colonists remembered and represented the disaster
the exact area burned in each district of the colony
the cause of the fires, which Strutt showed as lightning
Aboriginal burning practices in the Port Phillip District
questions.explanation: Painted thirteen years after the event, the work is a dramatic composition of settlers and animals fleeing, so it shows how the disaster was imagined and remembered. It cannot measure the burnt area, and it is not a record of Aboriginal burning.

questions.stem: In 1887 the Chaffey brothers began irrigation settlements on the Murray River at:
options: Mildura and Renmark
Shepparton and Echuca
Griffith and Leeton
Albury and Wodonga
questions.explanation: George and William Chaffey founded irrigation colonies at Mildura in Victoria and Renmark in South Australia. Griffith and Leeton belong to the later Murrumbidgee Irrigation Area in New South Wales.

questions.stem: Alfred Deakin's Irrigation Act 1886 (Victoria) was a turning point in water management because it:
options: banned irrigation in Victoria until a drought plan had been agreed
vested the right to use the water of rivers and streams in the Crown
gave landholders private ownership of the rivers running through their land
handed control of the Murray River to a new national water authority
questions.explanation: The Act replaced the English rule of riparian rights, under which landholders beside a stream had rights to its water, with Crown control. This allowed the state to plan irrigation trusts and schemes. There was no national government until 1901.

questions.stem: Alfred Deakin met George and William Chaffey, and encouraged them to bring their methods to Victoria, while studying irrigation in:
options: London, at a conference on the British Empire's water supply
California, where the brothers ran irrigation colonies
Ontario, Canada, where the brothers were born and farmed
Egypt, where the brothers had built canals along the Nile
questions.explanation: Deakin's Royal Commission tour of 1885 took him to the western United States, where the Chaffeys had founded irrigation settlements in California. The brothers were Canadian-born, which makes Canada a tempting but wrong answer.

questions.stem: Which long-term consequence of irrigation along the Murray River is best supported by later evidence?
options: Native fish numbers grew as channels created new habitat
Rising water tables brought salt to the surface of irrigated land
River flows increased because channels returned water to the river
Irrigation removed the need for dams and weirs on the Murray
questions.explanation: Heavy watering raised groundwater tables, carrying salt into the root zone and later into the river, so salinity became a major problem. Irrigation reduced river flows and depended on dams and weirs, which also harmed native fish.

questions.stem: The Federation drought, at its worst around 1901–02, had which effect on pastoral industries?
options: Huge stock losses, worsened by overstocking and rabbits stripping pasture
Rising sheep numbers as flocks were moved to coastal irrigated pasture
A collapse in wool prices caused by an oversupply of fleeces from Australia
Little loss of stock, because most stations already had irrigation
questions.explanation: Millions of sheep and cattle died as feed and water failed. Overstocked runs and rabbit plagues had already stripped the ground cover, which deepened the losses and the damage to the land. Few stations had any irrigation.

questions.stem: The colonies along the Murray argued over its water during the Federation debates of the 1890s. How did the Constitution respond?
options: Water was left out of the Constitution because no colony raised it
Commonwealth trade laws could not cut states' reasonable use of river water
The Commonwealth was given ownership of all inland rivers and their water
South Australia was given control of the Murray's flow below the border
questions.explanation: Section 100 says Commonwealth laws of trade or commerce must not abridge a state's right to the reasonable use of river waters for conservation or irrigation. Water was therefore left largely with the states, which shaped river management for a century.

questions.stem: The 'National Park' south of Sydney, set aside in 1879 and later renamed the Royal National Park, is often described as:
options: the first area in Australia put on the World Heritage List
the second national park in the world, after Yellowstone
the first national park in the world, ahead of Yellowstone
the first park run jointly with its Aboriginal custodians
questions.explanation: Yellowstone in the United States was declared in 1872, so the Sydney park of 1879 is usually called the world's second. Joint management with Aboriginal owners and World Heritage listing both came about a century later.

questions.stem: The main purpose given for reserving the 1879 National Park near Sydney was:
options: recreation and fresh air for Sydney's growing population
protecting endangered native species from extinction
preserving Aboriginal sacred sites from development
securing a clean water catchment for Sydney's supply
questions.explanation: The park was created as a place of healthy recreation for city workers. Early managers cleared areas for picnic grounds and introduced deer, which shows that preserving native species was not then the main aim.

questions.stem: Tower Hill, reserved in 1892 as Victoria's first national park, is:
options: a volcanic crater lake near Warrnambool
a granite range in the Grampians
a rainforest gully in the Dandenongs
a stretch of Murray River floodplain
questions.explanation: Tower Hill is a volcanic crater with a lake and islands near Warrnambool in south-western Victoria. Its reservation came after decades of clearing and grazing had stripped much of its vegetation.

questions.stem: From the 1960s Tower Hill was replanted using Eugene von Guérard's 1855 painting of the site as a guide to its earlier vegetation. This shows that:
options: colonial art can serve as evidence of past environments
the reserve had been protected from clearing since 1855
von Guérard painted the scene to persuade the colony to reserve it
no vegetation had been lost between 1855 and the 1960s
questions.explanation: Von Guérard's detailed landscape recorded plants that later disappeared, so restorers used it as a historical source. The replanting was needed precisely because the vegetation had been cleared after 1855.

questions.stem: In Aboriginal belief, custodianship of Country means that:
options: land belongs to whoever first clears and farms it
land may be sold to others once it has been cared for
only Elders may enter Country, which others must avoid
people belong to the land and have obligations to care for it
questions.explanation: Custodianship expresses a relationship in which people belong to Country and carry responsibilities, set out in law and ceremony, to look after it. The idea that clearing and farming create ownership is the European doctrine of improvement.

questions.stem: The legal idea later known as terra nullius shaped British colonisation of Australia because it treated the continent as:
options: land belonging to no one, so the Crown could claim it without a treaty
land conquered in war, so Aboriginal laws would continue under the Crown
land ceded by Aboriginal nations in return for protection by Britain
land held in trust by the Crown on behalf of its Aboriginal owners
questions.explanation: Australia was treated as a 'settled' colony, as if no one owned the land, so the Crown claimed sovereignty and ownership without treaties or purchase. Under British law a conquered territory kept its existing laws, which is why the conquest option is wrong.

questions.stem: In the semi-arid Western Division of New South Wales, heavy stocking in the 1880s, followed by rabbits and then the Federation drought, led to:
options: rising water tables that turned much of the western plains into permanent wetlands
the loss of saltbush and other perennial plants, soil erosion and a collapse in sheep numbers
a rapid recovery of native grasses once the sheep were moved to coastal runs for shearing
the spread of eucalypt forest across plains that had previously been open grassland
questions.explanation: Pastoralists stocked the dry western plains as if every season were a good one. Sheep and rabbits stripped the perennial saltbush and grasses, the soil eroded, and the drought then killed stock in huge numbers. Rising water tables and salinity were later problems of irrigation districts, not of these dry grazing lands.

questions.stem: The 'doctrine of improvement', drawn from writers such as John Locke, held that land became private property when people:
options: received it as a reward for service from the reigning monarch
mixed their labour with it by fencing, clearing and cultivating
inherited it through lines of family and kinship descent
held ceremonies on it and sang its stories over generations
questions.explanation: Locke argued that labour applied to land made it property. Colonists used this idea to claim that Aboriginal people, who did not fence or plough, had no ownership, ignoring the ways they actively managed Country.

questions.stem: The Selection Acts of the 1860s required selectors to live on, fence, clear and cultivate their blocks to keep them. Which idea about land does this condition best reflect?
options: Land should be held in trust for future generations
Land was best left in its natural state for wildlife
Land should be owned collectively by each district
Land was valued for what labour could make it produce
questions.explanation: Making title depend on clearing and cultivation reflects the doctrine of improvement and colonial ideas of progress: land was worth what it produced. Conservation and collective ownership were not the principles behind selection.

questions.stem: Colonial ideas of 'progress' in the 19th century usually measured a district's success by:
options: the survival of its native forests and wildlife
how much of it remained under Aboriginal management
how much land was kept as common grazing for all
its cleared acres, fenced paddocks, towns and exports
questions.explanation: Settler ideology celebrated clearing, fencing, building towns and producing wool and wheat for export as signs of civilisation and progress. Protecting forests and wildlife became a public value only gradually, late in the century.

questions.stem: Many Aboriginal men and women worked as stockmen, shepherds, trackers and guides on pastoral stations in the 19th century. Historians commonly interpret this as:
options: a requirement of the Victorian Half-caste Act across all colonies
proof that cultural practices had ended by the 1850s
a way of staying on Country while adapting to colonisation
evidence that Aboriginal people welcomed the pastoral takeover
questions.explanation: Station work let many people remain on or near their own Country, keep up kinship and ceremony and survive in a changed economy. It was an adaptation under pressure, not consent, and the Victorian Act of 1886 applied only in Victoria.

questions.stem: From the 1860s Wurundjeri and other Kulin people at Coranderrk cleared land, farmed, and grew hops for sale. This is best seen as an example of:
options: rejecting every European tool, crop and method of farming
leaving Country to work in Melbourne's growing factories
taking up European farming to secure land and independence
accepting that all rights to their Country had been extinguished
questions.explanation: Kulin leaders had sought land of their own, and Coranderrk's farming success showed they could use European methods to support themselves on a reserve they had chosen. This adaptation was a strategy for survival and independence, not surrender of their claims.

questions.stem: Before colonisation, many Torres Strait Islander communities, especially on the eastern islands, lived by:
options: trading greenstone axes from Victoria for pearl shell from New Guinea
gardening crops such as yams and taro, fishing and hunting turtle and dugong
herding cattle on cleared island pastures and trading hides to the mainland
growing irrigated wheat on the larger islands and storing grain in villages
questions.explanation: Islander communities such as those on Mer cultivated gardens and drew on the sea for fish, turtle and dugong, with land and sea held under customary law. Cattle and wheat were colonial introductions.

questions.stem: For many Aboriginal peoples, particular places on Country are sacred because:
options: they were granted by colonial governments as Aboriginal reserves
they mark the boundaries surveyed for pastoral runs
they are the oldest campsites anywhere in the region
they are linked to ancestral beings and the stories of creation
questions.explanation: Sacred sites are places where ancestral beings acted, rested or became part of the land, and the law connected with them is carried in story, song and ceremony. Their meaning comes from that relationship, not from age alone or from colonial grants.

questions.stem: A squatter in the 1840s describes his run as 'unoccupied waste land'. A Wurundjeri Elder describes the same area as Country for which his family is responsible. The best explanation of the difference is that the two men:
options: based their claims on improvement versus kinship and law
differed only about where the run's boundaries lay
both believed land could be sold but disputed the price
agreed the land was unused but disagreed over who saw it first
questions.explanation: The squatter judged land by European ideas of fencing, clearing and productive use, so country without these looked 'waste'. The Elder's claim rested on kinship, law and obligations to Country, so the disagreement is about what ownership means, not boundaries or price.

questions.stem: Painters of the Heidelberg School, such as Tom Roberts and Arthur Streeton, in the 1880s and 1890s depicted the bush mainly as:
options: a dark and threatening wilderness that settlers needed to clear
a landscape shaped by Aboriginal fire, painted to support land rights
an English-style countryside of hedges, lanes and green fields
a sunlit, distinctly Australian landscape tied to national identity
questions.explanation: Heidelberg School artists painted the light, heat and colours of the bush and the work of pastoral life, and their images became linked with a growing sense of Australian nationhood before Federation. This marked a growing appreciation of the local environment.

questions.stem: The Acclimatisation Society of Victoria, founded in 1861, aimed to:
options: eradicate rabbits and foxes from Victorian farms and gardens
introduce useful and familiar animals and plants from other lands
protect native animals from introduced predators such as foxes
return land to the condition it was in before colonisation
questions.explanation: Acclimatisation societies brought in species thought useful or reminiscent of home, such as birds, fish and game animals. Several became pests, the opposite of protecting native wildlife.

questions.stem: In 1859 Thomas Austin released wild rabbits on his property at Barwon Park near Geelong for:
options: food for gold miners
fur for the hat trade
grazing down weeds
hunting for sport
questions.explanation: Austin wanted game to shoot, as on an English estate. The wild rabbits spread across the south-east within decades, stripping pasture and contributing to erosion and the decline of native plants.

questions.stem: The extinction of the thylacine (Tasmanian tiger) is linked to colonisation in part because:
options: they were shipped overseas in large numbers for zoos and private collectors
the Tasmanian government paid bounties for killing them to protect sheep
gold miners hunted them for meat during the rushes of the 1850s
rabbits released in Victoria in 1859 carried a disease that killed them
questions.explanation: Graziers blamed thylacines for killing sheep, and a government bounty from 1888 to 1909 encouraged their slaughter, alongside habitat loss and disease. The last known thylacine died in a Hobart zoo in 1936.

questions.stem: By the late 1880s 'Marvellous Melbourne' faced serious pollution. The Melbourne and Metropolitan Board of Works was created in 1891 mainly to:
options: build a sewerage system for a city fouled by its own waste
plan national parks and gardens around the growing suburbs
irrigate market gardens on the flats along the Yarra River
build new railway lines to the gold towns of central Victoria
questions.explanation: Rapid urban growth had left Melbourne with open drains, polluted waterways and outbreaks of disease. The Board's task was water supply and sewerage, a response to the environmental cost of urbanisation.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates the consequences of colonial land use by 1901?
options: Food and wool output grew hugely while Aboriginal custodianship was severely disrupted
Change was limited because most of the land still remained under Aboriginal management
The environment was little changed because clearing was mostly confined to the towns
Aboriginal and colonial land use had merged into a single shared system of management
questions.explanation: By Federation colonists had built huge pastoral and farming industries and growing cities, while Aboriginal people across the south-east had lost most of their land and faced restrictions on caring for Country. Clearing, grazing and introduced species had changed the land far beyond the towns.

questions.stem: Which is the best example of continuity, rather than change, in the history of land in Australia between 1788 and 1901?
options: Many Aboriginal people kept caring for Country and culture where they could
The Crown continued to recognise Aboriginal ownership of unsettled land
Native animal and plant populations stayed largely stable in settled districts
Pastoralism remained confined to the county of Cumberland around Sydney
questions.explanation: Despite dispossession, many Aboriginal people maintained connection to Country, knowledge and practice, which is a strong thread of continuity. The Crown never recognised Aboriginal ownership in this period, native species declined, and pastoralism spread across much of the continent.
